articles.title: Local AI on a PC: what actually works (Whisper, translation, LLMs)
articles.excerpt: Local AI is the most overpromised topic in dev tooling. "Run GPT on your laptop" — sure, if your laptop has 12 GB of VRAM and you enjoy 3 tokens per second. I've been running local models in productio…
articles.body: Local AI is the most overpromised topic in dev tooling. "Run GPT on your laptop" — sure, if your laptop has 12 GB of VRAM and you enjoy 3 tokens per second. I've been running local models in production-ish settings for a while (speech recognition, translation, TTS, document analysis). Here is what actually works on consumer hardware, and what doesn't. Speech recognition: faster-whisper The best value-per-watt local model I use. CTranslate2 backend, int8 quantization. medium int8 on an RTX 2070: ~ 4.4 GB of VRAM , a 30-second fragment in 0.36–1.62 s depending on speech density; CPU works too, several times slower — fine for batch transcription, too slow for real-time subtitles; hallucination filter is mandatory: silence and noise produce plausible-looking text that nobody said.

articles.title: A sync server that cannot read your data (Raspberry Pi, 30 minutes)
articles.excerpt: Your password manager syncs through someone else's server. Mine syncs through a Raspberry Pi in my flat — and I can tell you exactly what that server can and cannot see. A sync server is a small servi…
articles.body: Your password manager syncs through someone else's server. Mine syncs through a Raspberry Pi in my flat — and I can tell you exactly what that server can and cannot see. The idea: a server that cannot read anything A sync server is a small service that accepts encrypted records and hands them to your other devices. The important part is what it does not have: no master password; no keys; no plaintext — only nonce, ciphertext and version metadata. That is the zero-knowledge model: the server is blind storage. If someone steals the Pi, they get ciphertext. If I forget the master password, the data is gone — and that's the honest trade-off, not a bug.

articles.excerpt: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its stellar companion.
articles.body: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA launches MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to investigate the planet's missing water. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars. The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago. MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars . The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere.

articles.title: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why
articles.excerpt: The answer to one of Earth's greatest geological mysteries may lie deep beneath our feet.
articles.body: More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished. Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past. Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth . Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years. But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.
